why: Only A holds: profit of £50m rises 10% to £55m over 141 products, which is £390,071 per product; C applies a 10% fall (£45m) and B and D are tenfold unit slips.
Only A holds: the percentage decreases are Q4 45.5%, Q3 33.3%, Q2 29.5%, Q5 26.9%, Q1 21.1%, giving 4, 3, 2, 5, 1 with no ties.
Only C holds: employees = (h+v)/165, so kg per employee = L×165/(h+v); D divides by 165 instead of multiplying, a trap.
C holds as the threshold: the proposal saves $14,000 + $27,600 = $41,600, which buys 2,773 assembler hours at $15, so 2,750 is the highest option that still pays and 3,200 does not.
Only C holds: H2 2010 profit index 149×99 = 14,751 beats H1 2010's 143×100 = 14,300 (even at a 98.75 reading), while A is 8.5 times (17 vs 2, both read exactly), B is about 7% and D is about 3.4%.
Only B holds: employees = (w+n)/38, so orders per employee = k×38/(w+n); A divides by 38 instead, a trap.
Only B holds: drops are Q2 45%, Q3 34.3%, Q5 27.8%, Q4 25%, Q1 14.3%, giving 2, 3, 5, 4, 1 with no ties.
D holds: claims not settled automatically are 41% of 618k = 253.4k versus 53% of 638k = 338.1k, a gap of 84.8k ≈ 85k; narrower readings (engine-only failures, about 33k) match no option.
Only B holds: sales per ad dollar are D 18.6, B 13.0, E 10.4, A 7.65, C 7.43, giving D, B, E, A, C.
D holds: April-May is 0.5×170×60/41 = 124.4 min per alteration and June is 2.5×170×60/187 = 136.4 min, a difference of about 12 minutes.
